events.title: Trump to Venezuela's Rodriguez: Elections need to happen
events.summary: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say. "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said. What they're saying: "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security," Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X. The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up. Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals. On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Marina Corina Machado went public to complain that she has been blocked from re-entering the country. In the Miami area, home to both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a sizable population of Venezuelan exiles and expats, former Democratic Senate candidate and Rep. Debbie Mucarsel Powell, posted the image on X and urged people to register to vote. "Tell every single member of the South Florida delegation that you are done with the lies and the blatant corruption. No Mas!" she wrote . Between the lines: The U.S. wants Venezuela's elections to be called by Venezuelans via the country's new National Reconciliation Council, which represents various political parties in the country. It's a three-step plan: Change the composition of the Venezuelan Supreme Court to make it more representative of the country. The opposition is going to get to nominate justices, an official said. Reform the National Electoral Commission to ensure there's not a repeat of 2024, when it manipulated the vote count and stole the election from Edmundo González on Maduro's behalf. Announce an election date. Trump, however, pointedly did not say when he wants that to be. Inside the room : Trump and Rodriguez were joined by two Venezuelan officials as well as Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Trump did most of the talking and also regaled Rodriguez with a description of the precision U.S. military operation that ousted Maduro. "It was warm. It was friendly. But it was also direct," one of the sources said about Trump's discussion of the importance of future elections. "She acknowledged it. She said she wants elections too," the source said. Zoom out: The multiple challenges Venezuela is facing from the legacy of socialist mismanagement to the earthquakes that damaged the country this summer make calling an election date even more complicated, U.S. officials say. "We don't want to have an election, have a democratically elected government take over and inherit an economic catastrophe within six months," said one. "A democratic government is going to be facing massive street protests over inflation, the economy. It could threaten the entire thing." The intrigue : By process of elimination, insiders say a Venezuelan election in the summer or fall of 2028 makes more sense because it would give the country more time to repair its finances and electoral system. Trump also would like to leave office with the legacy of removing a dictator, fixing a country and fostering democracy — but he might want to wait until the final months in office so the U.S. could still exert outsized influence on Rodriguez's government. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has called for Venezuela to hold elections on July 24, 2027, but Trump administration officials and allies say that might be too early. "If it can be in '27, that would be great. We would like that," an official said, cautioning that Venezuelans need to lead and need to fix their debt problem first. "Whether the date for those conditions to be met are 2027 versus 2028 is still up in the air," the official said. "It certainly can't go on indefinitely."

events.title: Why ASEAN’s coming digital economy trade agreement deserves your attention
events.summary: At a time when much of the world is building digital walls, Southeast Asia is trying something more ambitious: building a digital bridge. Earlier this year, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) concluded negotiations on the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, or DEFA—the world’s first comprehensive, region-wide agreement dedicated to the digital economy. The pact is expected to be signed at the ASEAN Summit this November, when leaders from the group’s 11 member states will converge in Manila. DEFA may sound like the sort of acronym-laden agreement that disappears quickly from the headlines. It should not. The agreement is an attempt to do for the key elements of modern digital trade—data, digital payments, e-commerce, online consumer protection, and AI—what trade agreements once did for ports, tariffs and containers: create common rules and standards to drive seamless commerce across borders. DEFA is an overlooked attempt to solve one of the digital economy’s defining problems: commerce is increasingly borderless, but the rules governing it are not. Signing the agreement will only be the first step; ASEAN’s 11 members will have much work to do to make DEFA work in practice. But if they succeed, they’ll show how different economies can integrate while still preserving their differences. Asia’s next great growth story won’t be a single country growing into “the next China.” It will be a region—ASEAN, in this case—finding ways to connect itself and reaping the rewards of that closer integration. Companies operating across Southeast Asia today must often navigate 11 different regulatory environments. Large companies may be able to shrug off those compliance costs, but for a small manufacturer in Bangkok or Surabaya, it can be the difference between serving one market and reaching many. DEFA aims to make that leap easier. If implemented well, it can give regional hubs greater reach, help global companies build more consistent operations across ASEAN, and allow small businesses to connect more readily with new customers, suppliers and partners beyond their home borders. The opportunity in ASEAN is immense. A benchmark study by Google, Temasek and Bain estimated that the region’s digital economy surpassed $300 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025. ASEAN’s own studies project that the region’s digital economy could reach $1 trillion by 2030 on its current trajectory—and potentially touch $2 trillion if policymakers implement DEFA rules expeditiously. These figures will only grow as ASEAN’s middle class comes into its own. As Wolfgang Fengler of World Data Lab underscored at Mastercard’s ASEAN Inclusive Growth Summit last year in Kuala Lumpur, Southeast Asia is now at a “middle-class majority” tipping point. By 2032, ASEAN’s middle class will have grown by 112 million. This middle-class cohort will shape ASEAN’s growth and digital consumption patterns for decades. But it will also bring about a deeper change that won’t show up in GDP figures. When people enter the middle class, they don’t just consume more. They expect more: better services, safer transactions, access to capital, protection from fraud, and room to grow their small businesses. That is why DEFA is so critical. Through rules that promote cross-border data flows, regional commerce, and harmonized cybersecurity standards, DEFA will help ASEAN embrace the modern-day digital economy. At the same time, it is sending a broader signal to policymakers and corporate leaders around the world: integration still matters, even in this age of tariffs, trade wars, and digital sovereignty. Since its founding in 1967, ASEAN has had to embrace both integration and diversity. Its membership includes advanced hubs like Singapore, emerging markets like Indonesia, and small island economies like Timor-Leste. ASEAN’s leaders have navigated this diversity by striving for commonality, not conformity, in how they bridge different systems. Global leaders should pay attention to DEFA, as it shows one way that regions can foster growth in the digital age without eroding trust, deepening inequality or stifling innovation. Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are eager to reach regional markets, yet they face uneven rules, fragmented payment systems, and different standards from country to country. Every additional layer of friction translates into forgone sales and lost revenue—not just for the business, but also for governments who see the digital economy as a key source of tax revenue. Of course, DEFA will not solve all these issues overnight. The hard work comes after the ink dries in Manila, and it will require policymakers, industry partners, and civil society to bring the agreement to life. The real litmus test will be how DEFA works for ordinary people and businesses. Can payments clear securely across borders? Can consumers participate online without falling prey to scammers ? Can small businesses sell beyond their home markets and grow cross-border orders? Assuming the agreement can deliver these outcomes, DEFA will be remembered as more than a diplomatic milestone. It will mark a moment when Southeast Asia asserted leadership in the digital domain. And if ASEAN’s bet pays off, it won’t just carry Southeast Asia into the digital future. It may show others how to get there too. events.title: How Meta took the lead in the race for the post-smartphone world
events.summary: There are moments when you experience emerging tech for the first time, and it feels genuinely different. That’s the case the first time you put on a pair of Meta’s most advanced smart glasses , which project a high-resolution digital box inside the right lens and allow you—with the help of a smart wristband—to control objects on the screen by moving your fingers. Tap your pointer finger and thumb together, and an app opens. Say, “Hey, Meta ,” and you’re suddenly chatting with an AI bot. This, as Meta sees it, is how most of us will eventually use AI. The company recently took Fortune inside a private demo room at its Menlo Park, Calif., headquarters to show off its growing family of smart glasses. The collection included the flagship Ray-Ban Wayfarer camera-enabled glasses, with an updated nine-hour battery life; the Ray-Bans with the lens display and “neural” wristband ; new audio-only smart glasses that ditch the built-in camera; new styles including Aviator frames; and prototypes like the Orion augmented reality glasses. Few companies have managed to crack the code for AI-enabled wearables—and specifically glasses—as Meta has. A strategic partnership with Ray-Ban parent EssilorLuxottica has played a major part, and despite widespread privacy concerns, Meta’s glasses are the most popular on the market. It’s a relatively small market, but one the tech industry is taking very seriously. Silicon Valley’s elite companies are racing to create hardware in new, AI-friendly “form factors,” betting that there are better ways for consumers to interact with AI—whether that’s through smart glasses or some yet-to-be-invented gadget. Leading AI labs such as OpenAI and, reportedly, Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are hard at work developing new devices. Musk disputes the report. Numerous smaller startups and industry giants like Apple are also working on new hardware . At a time when the race to build the best frontier models is center stage, the competition to establish the next hardware platform is shaping up to be just as important. At stake is control over how billions of people access AI, regardless of whose bots are the smartest. Meta’s lead Meta is a case in point. Its AI models generally lag those of rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic. But Meta stands above all in AI-enabled glasses , having grown its sales of smart glasses threefold last year; EssilorLuxottica says it sold 7 million pairs of AI-enabled glasses in 2025. Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables, credits the company’s early bet on the category and its decision to prioritize fashion. Customers use the smart features on the glasses only about 10% of the time, he said, so it’s critical that people crave the glasses for their look and weight. EssilorLuxottica held Meta to 50 grams or below for most glasses. “We’re able to keep adding this stuff into something that you’re already wearing for other reasons,” Himel said of the tech features. One new capability he’s excited about is agentic AI powered by Meta’s latest Muse Spark model , allowing the glasses to execute multistep routines like managing personal schedules and scanning through emails. Meta’s “Neural” wristband. WINNI WINTERMEYER for Fortune “As the AI gets better, you want something that’s always with you, can see what you see, hear what you hear,” Himel said. A new hologram feature scans your face and records your expressions, producing a 3D animated simulacrum of your visage. When you’re wearing the glasses and call a friend via Meta-owned WhatsApp, your hologram appears on their screen—and their hologram, if they have one, appears in your glasses. It’s impressive, but also a bit jarring: My hologram looked like a deepfake version of me. Meta on Wednesday also announced a new pair of virtual reality glasses that it says weigh only 100 grams and have capabilities for cinema display, gaming, spacial computing, and other features. The glasses, which the company says will ship in the spring, will cost $1,299. There are still rough edges. The glasses didn’t always respond to thumb swipes and sometimes lagged after voice commands. Meta’s AI also occasionally struggled to identify objects cleanly, such as when it attempted to calculate the number of calories in a trayful of food. The company pointed out that there is a natural learning curve and that the tech usually works for most people without issue. Meta’s Ray-Ban Display glasses start at $799, while its third-generation flagship camera-enabled Ray-Bans cost $449. The new audio-only glasses start at $349 and are shipping in two styles: The Ray-Ban Clubmaster and Burbank. The privacy problem The bigger concern surrounding this tech, however, is privacy. Already, Meta has had to respond to some users disabling the glasses’ LED light that turns on to alert people nearby that the video camera is recording. The company recently created a policy to deactivate recording if the LED has been tampered with , and Meta will delete the accounts of anyone who uses a modified device and posts harassing content. The Capri, one of Meta’s new style of glasses. WINNI WINTERMEYER for Fortune Stopping depraved users is only part of the challenge. The coolest features of AI devices come from AI’s ability to make sense of the world around you, operating not from on-screen data alone. That creates an inherent tension with norms around privacy and personal space. Recently announced Apple Watch features like Siri Recap, which listens to a user’s conversations and provides a “high-level” AI-generated summary, have already raised concerns about whether the audio is being captured with proper consent. OpenAI’s forthcoming device , rumored to be a portable smart speaker, could encounter similar eavesdropping concerns. So far, Meta’s famously poor privacy track record in social media has not prevented it from taking the lead in the nascent smart glasses category. But as the market grows, sensitivity around privacy is almost certain to become a bigger factor. Meta is already facing multiple proposed class-action lawsuits related to its smart glasses, including one alleging that it sent some footage captured by the glasses, including highly personal material, to third-party human reviewers for annotation and AI development. Meta disputes the allegations. Competitors, well aware of Meta’s reputation, are trying to win by making privacy central to their designs. AI startup Even Realities, which ditches audio or camera functions and focuses on text-only displays, began selling its smart glasses in 2024. Taiwan-based HTC Corp.’s Vive Eagle glasses tout a feature that turns off recording if anyone—not just the user—says, “Stop recording.” For its part, Meta is introducing private, isolated cloud “devices” to secure sensitive user data such as health information, and making some data processed through the glasses unreadable, even to the company. The US and China have bought themselves more time to negotiate. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that the countries had agreed to extend their trade truce from November 10 to January 10. He announced the extension after a meeting in Washington with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, as Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived for a state visit. "We will extend what we call the 'Busan Agreement,' the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on November 10, that is going to be extended until January 10," Bessent told Fox News during a live interview on Wednesday. The extra two months could lead to a broader deal, Bessent said, and the two sides could also "just roll the current deal" again. "There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we've sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement," Bessent said. events.title: SoftBank-backed Carro said to mull first dual Nasdaq-SGX IPO
events.summary: Carro has filed confidentially for an initial public offering in the US and recently submitted paperwork for a Singapore listing as well, people familiar with the matter said. Carro, a SoftBank-backed used-car marketplace, is considering a dual IPO listing on Nasdaq and Singapore Exchange's Global Listing Board, potentially raising $400-500 million. The dual-listing system allows companies to list simultaneously in the US and Singapore with a single set of documents, aiming to boost Singapore's market liquidity and company base. Singapore's IPO market shows growth but remains small compared to Hong Kong and India; initiatives include substantial fund allocations to support local stock investments. NEW YORK – Used-car marketplace Carro is considering offering shares on the Singapore Exchange’s Global Listing Board, people familiar with the matter said, potentially positioning it to be the first company to use the new dual-listing mechanism with Nasdaq Inc. Carro has filed confidentially for an initial public offering in the US and recently submitted paperwork for a Singapore listing as well, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The Singapore-based company, which is backed by SoftBank Group, could raise as much as US$400 million (S$510 million) to US$500 million, the people said. It is targeting a dual listing later in 2026 or in the first half of 2027, the people said. Deliberations are ongoing and details of the potential offering could change, according to the people. Carro could also decide against a Singapore listing depending on investor demand, they added. “The company considers and evaluates potential financing needs and opportunities from time to time and will make disclosures when appropriate to do so,” a spokesperson for Carro said in an e-mailed statement. Carro’s move is a boon for Singapore as it seeks to improve liquidity and broaden its base of publicly traded companies. Under the dual-listing system , which was first announced in 2025, companies need only prepare a single set of documents to float simultaneously in the US and Singapore, and the timing of their debuts will be aligned. Requirements include having at least S$2 billion in market value. DayOne Data Centers had also previously been considering a listing on SGX’s Global Listing Board that could have made it the first to use the new mechanism. The company has since decided not to pursue a concurrent dual listing and will instead focus on its US IPO for now, according to people familiar with the situation. DayOne confidentially filed for a US IPO in August and could raise US$5 billion, Bloomberg News has reported. It may still look to list in Singapore later, the people said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment. Singapore has not hosted a listing of US$1 billion or more since 2018, when South Korean internet company Kakao Corp. sold global depositary shares, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. IPOs in the city-state have fetched about US$1.1 billion in 2026 so far, a 33 per cent increase from the same period in 2025. While that is an improvement, largely thanks to UI Boustead REIT’s offering, it is a fraction of the proceeds in Hong Kong, which amounted to about US$48 billion, and India, which raised about US$11 billion. In other market initiatives, Singapore also set aside an initial S$5 billion in 2025 to be allocated to selected fund managers to invest in local stocks. In February 2026, it topped that up with another S$1.5 billion. BLOOMBERG

events.title: The timely tax strategy that can help bond investors make the best of runaway yields and big losses
events.summary: With the 10-year treasury yield surging above 5% and hitting its highest level since 2007. and bond prices suffering through a period of steep losses, investors who bought bond mutual funds or ETFs may be sitting on unrealized losses they can use to offset capital gains. Tax-loss harvesting in bonds is especially relevant now given the double-digit returns in stocks, and financial advisors say waiting until the end of the year to sell is not necessarily the best tax strategy, and that is even taking into account the recent Fed decision to raise interest rates, which could send yields higher. Fund companies including Vanguard Group and American Century Investments have been alerting investors to this tax strategy, though identification of individual fund positions with losses and analysis of the IRS wash-sale rule is critical. The bond market selloff has many investors licking their wounds, but it could also be a good time to take your losses as a tax advantage. With the 10-year treasury yield seeing a massive single-day spike on Wednesday, hitting its highest level since 2007, and bond prices continuing to fall, investors who bought bond mutual funds or ETFs when yields were lower may be sitting on unrealized losses within their portfolio. Investors often wait until December to tax-loss harvest — or sell investments at a loss and use their losses to offset gains in other investments. But you don't have to wait. The very thing hurting your bond ETF today — higher yields — can potentially give you both a tax asset and an opportunity to reinvest at a higher yield. "Tax-loss harvesting is often treated as a year-end exercise. But markets don't follow the calendar," senior portfolio managers Joseph Gotelli and Jason Greenblath wrote in a recent report for American Century Investments. "Today's fixed-income landscape offers compelling potential opportunities to harvest losses, manage tax liabilities and improve yield and tax efficiency." Taking a look at this tax strategy more often has been recommended in recent years amid persistent bond underperformance. "It's sensible to do tax-loss harvesting in client portfolios on a regular basis when opportunities arise," Vanguard Group wrote in an ETF industry perspective in the fourth quarter of last year. Vanguard cited bond price declines and record stock market highs, with the latter making any tax-loss harvesting in equities, "just about impossible to find." Here's what bond investors need to know about tax-loss harvesting to take advantage of the bond market selloff. Vanguard, iShares bond funds are among tax loss targets The recent selloff has given many investors an opportunity for tax-loss harvesting. Consider for instance, that the Vanguard Total Bond Market Index Fund ETF ( BND ) and the iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF ( AGG ) are both down more than 3.5% year to date. "It's an opportunity to strike while the iron's hot because there's no guarantee that these losses are going to stick around," said Conor Kelly, a partner and senior financial advisor with Prime Capital Financial in Overland Park, Kansas. "You don't want to wait until year-end because these losses could disappear or at least shrink." Kristin Larson, founder and wealth advisor at NewSpring Wealth Partners in Minnetonka, Minn., said tax-loss harvesting in bonds is especially relevant now given the double-digit returns in stocks. The S&P 500 , for instance, is up about 13% year-to-date. "For a lot of clients, the bond side of the portfolio is the only side that's down right now," Larson said. Cost basis analysis of the shares you hold is critical Don't look only at the current price of your fund to decide whether or not to sell. "It's not automatic that you'll have a tax loss just because an ETF has a negative price return for the year," said Bill Schwartz, managing director in the Potomac, Maryland, office of Wealthspire. For instance, if you bought the Vanguard Total Bond Market Index Fund ETF on Jan. 2 and didn't reinvest dividends or interest, you'd have a tax loss for the year to date because it has gone down in price. The ETF closed at 74.04 on Jan. 2 and was 71.40 on Sept. 21. "However, if you made multiple purchases over multiple years, there are no guarantees you'll have a tax loss," Schwartz said. REGISTER HERE. Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At Connect on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market. These glasses actually seem quite promising given their substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility. Moments before unveiling the VR glasses, MEta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile back to focus less on Metaverse and to build fewer VR devices until it has real breakthroughs. “This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.” The company says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal glasses than the bulky headsets that Meta previously released. Made of magnesium alloy, the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They are powered by a computing puck, which also acts as their battery. Presumably, a user can just slip the puck into their pocket, which allows the glasses to be used on the go. The glasses are largely entertainment-focused and come with micro-OLED panels built into the lenses, which provide a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, as well as Dolby Vision and support for Dolby Atmos audio. Users will be able to download and watch movies. Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films. Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever.” What does that mean? Meta maintains that their glasses will be one of the only ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines the distinct high-resolution viewing experience. The glasses are also compatible with 3D experiences — and even movies that integrate a user’s physical space is integrated into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that, in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D. Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience. The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures. events.title: I tried Meta's new $1,300 VR Glasses. They might be good for watching a movie — but I'm not sure what else.
events.summary: Meta's new VR Glasses are good for watching a movie, but I'm not sure what else you'd use them for. Business Insider Meta is showing off new VR Glasses, which will start selling next spring for $1,300. These are a much cheaper and lighter version of the Apple Vision Pro, which launched two years ago. But the Vision Pro flopped in part because people can't figure out what to do with them. Can Meta figure it out this time? Two years ago, Apple introduced its Vision Pro virtual reality goggles . They failed : They were too expensive, too heavy, and — crucially — no one could figure out what to do with them . Now Mark Zuckerberg is taking a swing at the same idea. The new Meta VR Glasses, which he debuted at his annual developers' conference Wednesday, are way cheaper and way lighter than Apple's, and they have at least one cool new feature. But I'm still not sure what to do with them. Meta's VR Glasses are connected to a puck. Meta The basics: The Meta VR goggles — which they've been working on for years — will go on sale in spring 2027 for $1,300 — a third of the Apple Vision Pro's starting price. The headset weighs about 100 grams — much, much less than the 600 grams the AVP weighs. (The Meta glasses also require a not-too-bulky "puck," which provides battery and computing power for the device. Meta expects the puck will sit next to you when you use the goggles, but you could also conceivably wear this thing on your belt if you wanted to stand up or (don't do this) walk around with the goggles on.) And at their core, Meta's goggles do the same thing as Apple's: Put them on and you can see a completely encompassing view of a virtual world. You can also toggle them so you can look outside into the real world, sort of*. Just like the Apple Vision Pro, it's quite an amazing experience, at least from a technical standpoint. The Meta goggles also improve on the " Minority Report " hand-wavy interface that both Apple and Meta have used before. Instead of having to hold your hands up in front of you to manipulate virtual stuff, like AVP requires, or use a wristband that reads the electrical impulses your hands make, like Meta's souped-up Ray Ban line, these goggles allow you to manipulate your surroundings with your hands when they are at your desk, or at your side, or in your lap. Super cool. But what would you actually do with these things if you owned them? The most obvious answer is "watch a movie." Which helps explain why "Avatar" director James Cameron has been working with Meta on these (and talking about them ) for some time. This is also the answer that Meta employees who are demoing the product give you. And I can definitely see why this might be more fun on a plane than watching a movie on my iPhone. On the other hand, I have to take my iPhone with me when I fly. Do I also want to bring a $1,300 pair of goggles with me? And if I'm not on a plane, then … this is where I get stumped. You don't want to wear these around anyone you actually want to talk to or interact with, for pretty obvious reasons. (This is also a privacy upside: You don't need to worry about people secretly recording you with these things , because anyone with eyes can see you're wearing a big piece of tech on your face. Zero chance you're sneaking up on anyone.) And if you're by yourself, at home, wouldn't you just watch a movie on a TV? Meta has other suggestions as well: You can play relatively crude games with these, similar to what Meta's existing Quest goggles let you do. You could also use it as a work device and pull up multiple screens to work on. And I do think there are a number of antisocial coders who might like this. And beyond that? You got me. I do understand why Meta, which has spent tens of billions of dollars working on consumer hardware , keeps plugging away at it, even though it has yet to create a truly mass-market success: Zuckerberg hopes that one of these devices will become the next version of the iPhone — a device lots of people use to access the internet, but one that he controls, instead of Apple or Google. This kind of tech also syncs nicely with the entire tech industry's AI push: Once you're wearing a face computer, it makes plenty of sense to bark commands at an attached AI, which is most definitely what Meta wants you to do with its goggles, too. But that AI push also means we could be looking at a future where the device you use matters a lot less than the AI you use. Meta's Muse agent app , for instance, appears to be a hit out of the gate, and I've been using it extensively on my iPhone. I'm sure Zuckerberg would prefer if I use Muse on his own hardware. But I'm also sure what's most important is that people use Muse . That doesn't mean that Meta is going to abandon hardware — they are pushing very hard with their line of souped-up Ray-Bans , which aren't nearly as robust, but double as actual glasses you might wear. But I do wonder if this is their last attempt to put a face computer on your head — at least until they can explain what you'd do with it . *Both Apple and Meta's goggles feature "pass through" tech, which means they are actually filming the world outside your goggles and giving you an ever-so-slightly pixelated view of that inside your goggles. events.title: Hands-on with Meta's next VR headset
events.summary: Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers. Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream. Yes, but: In order to slim down the size, the new Meta VR glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage. Zoom in: I spent about half an hour on Tuesday getting to use a prototype of the new specs, which are controlled through a combination of eye-tracking, hand gestures and voice commands. Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro. Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done. I played a re-imagined version of Beat Saber that cleverly re-maps the music game for control via hand motions. I watched a clip from last year's NBA finals. I used a trio of virtual monitors to do some "vibe coding" on a website, with one display showing the Muse terminal and another previewing the site itself. Meta sees these VR glasses as a "general device," Meta VP of product Angela Chang told Axios. "It's not built for any specific use case per se." My thought bubble: It's the most practical combination I've seen of an Apple Vision Pro-class device in a headset I'd be willing to wear outside of the house. The big picture: Google is working on a similar device, known as Project Aura, set to debut later this year and built in partnership with Xreal. Meta touts its wider field of view and higher optical quality, among other advantages over Aura. Between the lines : As for why it won't arrive until next spring, Meta executives say they want to be sure it makes a good first impression, especially inside a VR ecosystem. "We really are trying to strive for a very high bar on the software quality and experience side," Chang said. Bottom line : Meta said it has modest expectations for unit sales, but says success will look like attracting folks beyond gamers, Chang said. "Are we bringing in new people into VR who, you know, maybe in the past would have looked at the Quest and said, 'Nah, that's not for me?'"

events.title: Meta's camera-free AI glasses look like regular Ray Bans
events.summary: The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, which don't include cameras and look a lot more normal. Meta Meta unveiled the Ray-Ban Meta Audio at its big conference. The two styles will have no camera — just audio and AI features. They start at $349, but not dealing with 'pervert glasses' backlash? Priceless. Great news for folks who enjoy the convenience of being able to listen to music or podcasts on their Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, but don't want to get frog-marched out of the gym locker room: Meta is launching a new audio-only version of its smart glasses that ditch the cameras. These glasses, which come in two styles — Burbank and Clubmaster — will start at $349. They ship October 13. Meta's new audio-only glasses without cameras. Pretty sleek compared to their camera siblings. Meta The audio-only versions still have the AI features. You can ask Meta's AI for things like a restaurant recommendation while you're walking around. You can also talk in real time with Meta's new AI agent, Muse, through the glasses . From my own testing of earlier Meta glasses, I can say that the audio features were one of my favorite aspects. Unlike earbuds or headphones, you weren't cut off from hearing your surroundings. This was great for specific contexts, like biking or walking outside, where I wanted to be able to hear traffic or other sounds for safety reasons. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses don't have cameras embedded in their frame. They look like regular Ray-Bans from the front. Meta You can also make hands-free phone calls, or listen and respond to text messages. The potential downside here is that, compared to taking a phone call on an AirPod, no one can see you've got anything in your ear, so it'll really seem like you're just talking to yourself in public. But that's your burden to bear. Ditching the camera has two big advantages. The first is the form factor: Without cameras, the frames can be lighter and therefore more comfortable (43 grams compared to 51 grams for the Gen 2 Wayfarer camera version). The audio-only glasses are also more stylish looking, with that classic flair in the corner of the Ray-Ban model where the camera would go. From the front, they look like regular Ray-Bans. Meta's new audio-only Clubmaster style glasses. Meta The second advantage is well, you're not wearing a device capable of filming people — which is what spawned the "pervert glasses" backlash to Meta's AI glasses. People understandably feel uncomfortable about the idea of being filmed without their awareness. Even though yes, people can film you on a phone, and yes, there is an LED indicator light , there's no doubt that the Meta glasses are much more subtle than filming with a phone, and many people don't notice that they're being filmed at all. Part of the bad perception of the Meta glasses has come from the kinds of videos that have gotten popular on social media filmed with the glasses. Pickup artists talking to women on the street and prank video makers harassing Walmart or other retail employees while wearing glasses became the two dominant types of content. This summer, Instagram announced it would crack down on the pickup artists , and started removing videos and sometimes even whole accounts of people who posted those videos (though as I previously reported, the enforcement has been somewhat spotty ). Businesses have responded to the backlash, too. Nightclubs, restaurants , and other places have started banning people from wearing Meta glasses inside. Events like the Rhode Island Comic-Con and the DEFCON security conference have also made rules banning Meta glasses. It'll be interesting to see if the camera-free version of Meta's AI glasses sell as well as their more expensive — and more capable — counterparts with cameras. Glasses with a built-in speaker are nifty — and these might appeal to people who otherwise would never want to buy smartglasses with a camera. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to its glasses
events.summary: Meta glasses. Meta Meta is betting its glasses can become a new front door for its fast-growing Muse AI agent. Meta is making a broader hardware push that includes audio glasses and a forthcoming VR device. AI agents are still imperfect, and sites like Amazon are pushing back. Meta is bringing its hot new AI agent Muse to its smart glasses. The move, announced Wednesday at its annual Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, gives Meta a new way to put Muse directly in front of users throughout the day. Muse has become a fast-rising entrant in the increasingly competitive AI agent market: software that can take actions on a person's behalf, rather than merely answer questions or generate text. Instead of opening an app or sitting down at a computer, people could eventually ask Muse for help through a pair of glasses already on their face. With a connection to your Muse personal AI agent, Meta's glasses "offer more ways than ever to help you manage daily life, whether you're building healthy habits or navigating a busy calendar, all without reaching for your phone," the company said in an announcement. At Connect, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company will "start upgrading the AI experience on Meta glasses" in the coming weeks. The announcement makes clear that the company sees its hardware business as important for the agent, which launched earlier this month and quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts , beating rivals like ChatGPT. Meta's broader hardware blitz at Connect also included Ray-Ban Meta Audio, a new audio-focused pair of glasses. It said it expects to offer more than 100 styles across Ray-Ban, Oakley, and Meta Glasses by the end of the year. It also announced Meta VR Glasses , which it said will offer a more immersive way to watch movies, play games, and work in virtual reality, and will go on sale next spring. Meta is waging a bigger battle over AI agents. Already, Muse can browse the web, make calls, shop, and handle other chores. Meta has also announced partnerships with companies including Shopify, PayPal, Expedia, and Instacart. That puts Meta in a heated race with startups such as Instinct, an invite-only personal AI assistant founded by 23-year-old Noah Shinn. Instinct launched before Muse and quickly caught on with Silicon Valley, turning the tiny startup into an unlikely rival for Meta. Personal AI agents are still early products, with uneven results. In a recent hands-on review, Business Insider's Katie Notopoulos found that Muse could help organize an inbox and identify subscriptions, while it struggled with school forms, medical scheduling, and some online checkouts. Muse also faces resistance from the websites and services they are meant to navigate. Earlier this week, Amazon blocked Muse from its shopping site, signaling that some companies may not embrace agents as readily as users do. Have a tip? events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349. While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained. This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. “Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses. Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed. The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted. Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life. The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said. All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data. events.title: Qld council says costs prevent it hitting recycling targets
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rockhampton Council warns escalating costs prevent it hitting recycling targets Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Tony Williams is calling on the Queensland government to help cover the costs of transporting recyclables for processing. ( Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council ) The Rockhampton Regional Council is calling on the state government for a subsidy to help cover the growing cost of transporting recyclables to the south-east corner for processing. Mayor Tony Williams says the council cannot achieve state-imposed recycling targets as it struggles to attract another company to develop a materials recovery facility locally. The Queensland government is designing a new fund to be spent on helping regional councils send recycling for processing. A regional Queensland council is warning it cannot meet state-imposed recycling targets with the growing cost of moving materials hundreds of kilometres for processing. Each year 10,000 tonnes of household recyclables collected from the Rockhampton region are driven 600 kilometres to a facility on the Sunshine Coast. Waste services cost the local council $3 million per year with more than one-third of that bill going to transportation fees. In June, the Queensland government released its waste strategy and set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035 , with major regional communities including Rockhampton expected to halve the amount of waste it sent to landfill. The Queensland government has set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035. ( ABC News: Ellie Willcox ) Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams said his council was struggling to improve recycling rates, especially as fuel prices soared. "We've done our waste plans and [our staff] are saying that we can't achieve the targets that the state government is putting onto councils," he said. Recyclables from central Queensland households were previously processed at a private materials recovery facility in Rockhampton. But that was destroyed by a battery fire in 2020. The council has so far been unable to attract private companies to develop a similar facility. The council has been unable to find a firm to develop a materials recovery facility locally. ( ABC Radio Canberra: Jolene Laverty ) Mayor Williams said the local government spent about $300 per tonne to send its recyclables for processing, compared to about $100 a tonne for councils in south-east Queensland. "The cookie-cutter approach to increasing recycling really doesn't help when the tyrannies of distance and the cost to transport that material is ever-increasing," he said. "With the state government wishing to increase recycling locally, there's no real [financial] benefit unless we get some subsidies towards those transport costs." In a statement, state environment minister Andrew Powell said the government was providing support for recycling in regional areas, with $11 million in new funding for infrastructure. The government was also designing a new fund to be spent on helping regional councils send recycling for processing. The state government is hoping a new fund can help regional councils send recycling for processing. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale ) Australian Council of Recycling chief Suzanne Toumbourou said the federal government should never have shelved national packaging reforms , which would have eased the burden on regional communities. "It's extraordinarily disappointing to see that lack of progress in packaging reform," Ms Toumbourou said. "We should have had regulatory certainty about the fact that burden would be shared much better across the supply chain and much more responsibility would be placed on producers." In a statement, federal environment minister Murray Watt said the government's focus was to work with state and territory governments to reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia.

events.title: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year. Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity , staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange. During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral. Vogue World Milano ends (appropriately Europoor-kitschily) with tiny robottini dancing to L’Amour Toujours while Alessandro Michele slowly dies inside pic.twitter.com/xicYWWl6VW I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves , and for falling and breaking .) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now. Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI. It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now. miuccia prada when the fuckass robot walked out during vogue world pic.twitter.com/SebwpV0zkl We are all Alessandro Michele, sitting front row at Vogue World Milan, having an existential crisis about the absolute state of things while robots awkwardly dance about. Numb to the pain at this point. Madness. just got off the phone with the creative director of Vogue World. First question he asked me. “So you hated the robots?” 🤭 Full interview on Substack tomorrow 👀 https://t.co/FTa3gumPgY — Louis Pisano (@LouisPisano) September 23, 2026 “I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?” One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala. “Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said. Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural. Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech. She points to the artist duo AA Murakami , who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala .

events.title: Exclusive: Thune plans another leader bid as Senate GOP fights to survive
events.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office. Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate. "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios. "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations. Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026. 🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself. And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said. Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues. 🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is " don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state." That could lead to a rebuke of Trump when Democrats force another vote on an Iran war powers resolution, expected before the Senate breaks for October. People's views have "evolved and changed" as the war has dragged on, he said. Many senators are "responding to what they're hearing back home." "That's a really hard vote," Thune acknowledged. " Any time you are committing your country to putting young men and women in harm's way — those are the hardest votes you'll make." He hopes Republicans will stick together to win the vote. What to watch: Thune wants to give Republicans more votes before the break to champion back home. He sees an opportunity with permitting reform legislation, which is being negotiated behind the scenes. Thune said it's possible he sets up a procedural vote on it after the final vote on the Protect College Sports bill. Thune is also floating a vote on the House-passed legislation targeting data center energy costs if the Senate remains in town next week. 💰 3. Spend cash like crazy: The Thune-linked Senate Leadership Fund is set to spend nearly $280 million in video advertising this year — more than any other group, according to AdImpact. Texas PAC, which is affiliated with SLF, is on track to spend another $112 million. " Texas is expensive ," Thune said, but "we're doing everything we can to help. We can't afford to lose Texas." The bottom line: "That's ultimately up to the conference," Thune emphasized when asked if he'd run again if the GOP lost the majority, but "that's the plan." "The elections are going to be really important — I think – in how we view what happens next." Thune said you can't "rule anything in or out" when asked if he could face a challenger for the position. "But I think we worked really hard to create an environment here that is conducive to individual senators being able to achieve their objectives," he said. "I think, in this job, you have to be a good listener."

events.title: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
events.summary: A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer , rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud. Why it matters : The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes. Zoom in : In his ruling, Judge Scott Beatle said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment . "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beatle wrote. "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote. What they're saying : "Today is a victory for the First Amendment—and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy. We are gratified that the Court recognized what this meritless lawsuit sought to obscure: that claims of "fake news" are little more than an attempt to punish news outlets for coverage those in power do not like," said Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA TODAY Co, Chief Legal Counsel. "A free press is fundamental to an informed public and a vibrant democracy. This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action." The big picture : The lawsuit is part of a broader effort by Trump and his Administration to target media companies with legal action for what they believe is unfair coverage. To date, the courts have mostly sided with media companies, citing the strength of the First Amendment. What we're watching: The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal lawyers, who did not respond when asked whether they plan to appeal.

events.title: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
events.summary: Farmer Steve Cargil is now paid $200,000 a year for hosting a solar farm on his land Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953. Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father. But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm. Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight. "I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says. Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on. Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm. "Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing. The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life." Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms. , external And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Solar farms can stretch out across the flat lands of Texas On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association. He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population. Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%, , external making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation. "We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says. Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state. "No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says. Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free. "We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long. By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration. Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land. Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent. Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says. Texas is now the largest producer of solar farm power in the US Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth. BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property. He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries. David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required.

events.title: 'Proteinflation': Meet the people paying up to £100 for a bag of protein
events.summary: The cost of the whey protein Amarpreet Singh buys has almost tripled since 2020 Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16. The 30-year-old, who lives in London and works in banking, started going to the gym at a time when he says protein supplements were mostly associated with bodybuilders. Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive. He says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020. By last year, the price had gone up to £120, though he managed to get one from eBay for £90. Among his gym friends, the rising prices have even been given a nickname – "proteinflation". Student Evie says the tub she buys is quite expensive for the size of it Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base, while food manufacturers now offer high-protein versions of everything from bagels to water. Evie Lewis is a more recent buyer of protein powder. The 19-year-old University of Manchester student began using it a few months ago because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet. "You hear a lot more about protein now on social media," she says. But at £32.99 for a 420g tub, she's feeling the high price and tries to make the product stretch. "I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested," she admits. Max Longman, 32, from Manchester, works in real estate and has been taking protein supplements for 10 years, originally to help him gain weight. He now drinks a protein shake every day and says his monthly spending on whey protein has risen from around £45 a year ago to £60 now. "Loads of foods have protein added to them now. Up until a few years ago, I'd never heard of high-protein yoghurt, and now I eat it three or four times a week," he says. Max Longman has been taking protein supplements for 10 years More recently, weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have added another source of demand. People taking these drugs typically eat less, and are often encouraged to make sure they get enough protein while losing weight to help preserve muscle. But that growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem - supply has not kept pace. And the result has been a sharp rise in the wholesale price of some key ingredients, and consumers are feeling the squeeze. High whey protein prices take chunk out of THG profits Published 6 August 2025 Food firms scramble to meet the high-protein craze Published 7 October 2025 According to global market intelligence platform Expana, the European price of one widely used type of high-protein whey was 130% higher in late August than a year earlier, and more than four times its level three years ago. There is no equivalent UK measure, but Expana says the UK market is closely linked to mainland Europe, where some British businesses source their whey protein. Other dairy proteins have also become more expensive, with another type of whey protein up 60% over the year, while one type of milk protein concentrate was up 80%. Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment. So some are starting to adapt what they make, by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein. Kieran Fisher's company Warrior is launching a product using cheaper sources of protein Warrior, a UK sports nutrition company, is one of those looking for alternatives. "Our whey protein powder was £12.50 on the shelf last year. We've put that up to £17.99 and we're still subsidising that from other aspects of the business," says its founder Kieran Fisher. The company is now launching a product using other sources of protein, which Fisher says costs around half as much as whey. The effects are also being felt outside the fitness market. Dairy proteins are used in infant formula, and Expana says higher dairy protein costs have contributed to price rises there too. There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust. Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago. For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max. "It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says. "If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly." But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story. "It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says. Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag.

events.title: Historic winery sold to Victorian company with plans to restart production
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Seppelt Wines sold to Stonier in Treasury Wine Estates sell-off The massive Seppelt sign is a renowned landmark adjacent to the Western Highway at Great Western. ( Supplied: Treasury Wine Estates ) Seppelt Wines has been sold to the family-owned Mornington Peninsula business Stonier Wines. It is the first brand to be sold off by wine giant Treasury Wine Estates as it slashes its wine portfolio. Stonier plans to start winemaking at the Seppelt winery in western Victoria and utilise its heritage-listed underground wine cellars. One of Australia's oldest and most renowned wineries has returned to private ownership. Family-owned Stonier Wines purchased Seppelt Wines from publicly listed wine giant Treasury Wine Estates. The sell-off is part of Treasury's plan to reduce its portfolio from 76 wine brands to fewer than 30. The sale includes Seppelt's vineyards and winery at Great Western, in western Victoria, and its Drumborg vineyard near Portland in south-west Victoria. The company bought the business for an unknown sum, with the sale expected to be finalised in mid-October. The Seppelt brand was launched by the Seppelt family in South Australia in 1851, and in 1918 the family acquired Hans Irvine's vineyards at Great Western. Stonier Wines is one of the pioneering estates on the Mornington Peninsula and returned to local family ownership in 2022. Stonier chief executive officer and co-owner Aaron Drummond said he was attracted to Seppelt after having worked in the Great Western wine region at the Mount Langi Ghiran winery for many years. Aaron Drummond says his business has big plans for Seppelt. ( Supplied: Aaron Drummond ) "It was incredibly exciting to see the potential of the region," he said. The sale includes the winery at Great Western, which has been largely dormant since 2014, but is expected to be restarted by Stonier. "The winery facility is a considerable facility that was processing about 8,000 tonnes a year but is currently crushing nothing," Mr Drummond said. "Our hope is to put a couple of thousand tonnes through that facility." Stonier will also make commercial use of Seppelt's historic underground cellars, which have been largely a tourist attraction in recent years. "We want to get them working again," Mr Drummond said. "They're the most phenomenal natural cooling environment, so it makes sense to us, and so we'll store all our top sparkling wines in them." "The Drives" in Great Western is the largest underground cellaring system in Australia, covering 3 kilometres. ( Supplied ) Treasury Wine Estates bought Seppelt in 2011, as part of the acquisition of Foster's Group's entire wine division. In June this year, the company announced plans to slash its brand portfolio in a cost-cutting exercise. Seppelt is the first brand to be sold off since that announcement. Angus Lilley, TWE's managing director for Australia, New Zealand and Europe, said the company was pleased to find a buyer in Stonier. "Seppelt holds a distinctive place in Australian wine, with a proud history shaped by generations of winemakers, viticulturists and people across the business and its local communities," he said. "For the people who know and love Seppelt, it's a positive move that keeps the brand in Victorian hands." Production will resume at the Great Western winery under Stonier. ( Supplied: Treasury Wine Estate ) Stonier's purchase of Seppelt comes at a time when the wine industry is under siege from falling global demand, historic oversupply, and low prices. Mr Drummond said while conscious of those challenges, he was positive about the future of the industry. "The wine industry is in probably the toughest cycle it's been in for a few decades, but the reality is that if you get the farming right and you get the wine quality right, the premium wine market is going ok, and there is growth," he said. He said Stonier was focused on quality over quantity. "Trying to make more wine doesn't make sense, but making better wine that can compete at a global level and really focusing on fine wine — I think there's a really lovely market for us," he said.
